rca-cert-expiry.summary: Produce requests are failing on all three brokers since 02:50Z, driven by SSL handshake failures from specific producer clients starting at 02:45Z. The cluster infrastructure (replication, controller, resources) is healthy; the issue is isolated to client-side authentication.

findings.title: Expired or invalid SSL certificates on producer clients causing handshake failures
findings.detail: The root-cause window shows a clear temporal sequence: SSL handshake errors from specific producer clients (app-2, app-3, app-5) began at 02:45Z (L1), immediately followed by a spike in FailedProduceRequestsPerSec on all three brokers at 02:50Z (M1, M2, M3). The errors are specific to the SSL listener (port 9093) and originate from client-side NetworkClient logs, indicating the brokers are rejecting the connections due to authentication failure. Since the errors are concentrated on specific client IDs rather than all clients, this points to a client-side certificate issue (e.g., expiration or revocation) rather than a broker-side configuration change.
findings.confirm_by: Check the validity and expiration dates of the SSL certificates used by the producer clients (app-2, app-3, app-5). Verify if any recent deployments or certificate rotations occurred for these specific applications around 02:45Z.

findings.title: Sustained produce request failures on all brokers
findings.detail: FailedProduceRequestsPerSec has departed from baseline (0) and remains elevated at ~18-22 requests/sec on kafka-0, kafka-1, and kafka-2 (M1, M2, M3). This is causing a 'Failure rate increase' problem (P1) and indicates that producers relying on SSL are currently unable to write to the cluster.
findings.confirm_by: Monitor the FailedProduceRequestsPerSec metric to see if it recovers after the client certificate issue is resolved.

findings.title: Intermittent consumer coordinator loading warnings
findings.detail: WARN logs indicate 'The coordinator is loading' for the orders-consumer group (L2). These warnings have occurred sporadically over the last 24 hours (01:07Z, 02:52Z) and are not strictly correlated with the SSL failure spike. This may indicate minor instability in the group coordinator or frequent rebalances, but it is not the primary cause of the current produce failures.
findings.confirm_by: Check consumer group rebalance logs and coordinator logs for the 'orders' group to determine if frequent rebalances are occurring.

recommendations.title: Inspect and rotate SSL certificates for affected producer clients
recommendations.rationale: The SSL handshake failures are isolated to specific producer clients (app-2, app-3, app-5) starting at 02:45Z. This strongly suggests their certificates have expired or become invalid. Rotating these certificates will restore connectivity.

recommendations.title: Review certificate expiration monitoring and alerting
recommendations.rationale: The failure occurred without prior warning in the provided digest. Implementing proactive monitoring for client certificate expiration dates can prevent future outages.

rca-consumer-deploy.summary: Consumer lag on orders-consumer spiked to ~103k records starting 02:40Z, driven by poll-timeout warnings that began at 02:22Z. The cluster itself is healthy (no replication, controller, or saturation issues). The root cause is a consumer-side processing bottleneck causing rebalance storms, likely triggered by a recent deployment or increased message complexity.

findings.title: Consumer processing bottleneck causing poll timeouts and rebalance storms
findings.detail: The timeline shows poll timeout warnings (L1) starting at 02:22Z, preceding the consumer lag spike (M1) at 02:40Z. These timeouts indicate the consumer application is taking longer than `max.poll.interval.ms` to process messages, causing the broker to evict the consumer from the group. This triggers a rebalance, which pauses consumption and causes lag to accumulate. The 'coordinator is loading' errors (L3) are a secondary effect of these frequent rebalances.
findings.confirm_by: Check if a deployment or configuration change occurred on the orders-consumer application around 02:20Z. Review consumer logs for processing exceptions or slow downstream dependencies (e.g., database latency) during the 02:22Z-02:40Z window.

findings.title: Active consumer lag alert on orders-consumer
findings.detail: Consumer lag has increased by 1157% compared to the prior 7-day average, reaching a maximum of 103k records. This is an active problem (P1) impacting the orders-consumer group.
findings.confirm_by: Monitor lag recovery after addressing the poll timeout issue. If lag does not decrease, check for consumer group stability.

findings.title: Intermittent network errors on brokers
findings.detail: Log template L2 shows 'Unexpected error from /<ip>' on brokers, occurring sporadically over the last 24 hours. While not directly correlated with the lag spike timeline, these errors could indicate network instability or client-side connection issues that may exacerbate consumer instability.
findings.confirm_by: Correlate these errors with specific client IPs and check for network packet loss or TCP resets on the broker nodes.

recommendations.title: Investigate consumer application performance and deployment history
recommendations.rationale: The poll timeouts (L1) are the primary driver of the lag. The application is likely spending too much time in `poll()` processing messages, possibly due to a recent code change, increased message size, or slow downstream dependencies.

recommendations.title: Review consumer configuration for rebalance stability
recommendations.rationale: To mitigate the impact of processing delays, consider increasing `max.poll.interval.ms` or reducing `max.poll.records` to allow more time per batch. If the application supports it, enable cooperative rebalancing or static membership to reduce the impact of rebalances.

rca-controller-quorum.summary: The cluster is experiencing a critical availability incident driven by controller quorum instability. Broker-to-controller heartbeat RPC timeouts on kafka-1 triggered a cascade of leader elections across all brokers, resulting in 4 offline partitions on kafka-0. The root cause appears to be network or controller quorum degradation starting at 02:28Z, rather than a broker crash or resource exhaustion, as replication and saturation metrics remain quiet.

findings.title: Controller Quorum Instability via Heartbeat RPC Timeouts
findings.detail: The incident timeline begins with BrokerLifecycleManager heartbeat RPC timeouts on kafka-1 at 02:28Z (L1). This loss of connectivity to the controller quorum likely caused the controller to mark kafka-1 as unresponsive, triggering a burst of leader elections across all three brokers (kafka-0, kafka-1, kafka-2) at 02:35Z (M2, M3, M4). This election storm subsequently led to offline partitions on kafka-0 at 02:55Z (M1, B1). The fact that UnderReplicatedPartitions and UnderMinIsrPartitionCount remain quiet (digest 'quiet' section) suggests the brokers themselves are healthy and data is not being lost due to disk or replication lag, but rather due to the controller's inability to maintain a stable quorum or assign leaders correctly.
findings.confirm_by: Check network latency and packet loss between kafka-1 and the controller nodes (kafka-0/2) between 02:28Z and 02:35Z. Verify if the controller quorum (ZooKeeper or KRaft) experienced leader changes or session timeouts during this window.

findings.title: Offline Partitions on kafka-0
findings.detail: There are currently 4 offline partitions on kafka-0 (M1, B1). This means data on these partitions is unavailable for read/write operations. This is a direct consequence of the leader election storm and potential failure to assign new leaders for these partitions. The problem P1 'Multiple infrastructure problems' confirms active availability impact.
findings.confirm_by: Identify which topics/partitions are offline on kafka-0. Check if these partitions have healthy replicas on other brokers that can be elected as leaders. If replicas are available, a manual leader election or controller restart (if stable) might resolve this, but root cause must be addressed first.

findings.title: Network Selector Errors Preceding Incident
findings.detail: Log template L2 shows 'Unexpected error from /<ip> ... closing connection' on all three brokers. While these errors occurred over a wider window (2026-10-11T06:48Z to 2026-10-12T03:55Z), the frequency on kafka-1 and kafka-2 in the hours leading up to the incident (02:22Z-02:53Z) may indicate underlying network instability or socket exhaustion that contributed to the heartbeat timeouts (L1).
findings.confirm_by: Correlate the specific IPs in L2 with the controller nodes. Check broker network metrics (socket counts, TCP retransmits) for kafka-1 and kafka-2 during the 02:00Z-03:00Z window to see if network saturation or errors preceded the heartbeat timeouts.

recommendations.title: Investigate Network Connectivity to Controller Quorum
recommendations.rationale: The primary trigger was heartbeat RPC timeouts (L1) leading to leader election storms (M2-M4). This suggests a network partition or latency spike between brokers and the controller quorum.

recommendations.title: Review Controller Quorum Configuration and Health
recommendations.rationale: If the network is stable, the controller quorum itself (ZooKeeper or KRaft) may be unstable. Check for controller leader changes or session timeouts in the controller logs during the 02:28Z-02:35Z window.

recommendations.title: Evaluate Broker Network Stack and Socket Limits
recommendations.rationale: The presence of Selector errors (L2) across all brokers suggests potential network stack issues or socket exhaustion that could exacerbate heartbeat timeouts under load.

rca-disk-full.summary: Broker aks-kafka-pool-0002 (kafka-2) has filled its data disk to 100%, causing log directory failures and subsequent under-replication on the remaining brokers. The cluster is currently degraded with active availability and durability risks.

findings.title: Disk exhaustion on aks-kafka-pool-0002 caused LogDirFailure and subsequent under-replication
findings.detail: The root cause is disk space exhaustion on the host aks-kafka-pool-0002. Disk usage departed from baseline at 02:30Z (M3) and reached 100% (B1). This directly caused 'No space left on device' errors in the Kafka log directory (L1) starting at 02:42Z. The failure of the log directory on kafka-2 led to it being unable to serve replicas, resulting in Under-Replicated Partitions (URP) appearing on the surviving brokers kafka-0 (M1) and kafka-1 (M2) at 03:00Z. The 'Process unavailable' problem (P1) likely reflects the impact of this broker failure on the cluster's availability.
findings.confirm_by: Verify that the disk usage on aks-kafka-pool-0002 is indeed 100% and that the Kafka process on that node is either down or unable to write to its data directory. Check if the URP count on kafka-0 and kafka-1 correlates with the partitions hosted on kafka-2.

findings.title: Broker aks-kafka-pool-0002 disk at 100% capacity
findings.detail: The disk usage on aks-kafka-pool-0002 has reached 100% (M3, B1, B2). This is a critical condition that prevents Kafka from writing new data or checkpoint files, as evidenced by the LogDirFailureChannel errors (L1). This is the primary driver of the current incident.
findings.confirm_by: Inspect the disk usage on aks-kafka-pool-0002 to confirm the 100% usage and identify which files or directories are consuming the space.

findings.title: Active Under-Replicated Partitions on kafka-0 and kafka-1
findings.detail: Both kafka-0 and kafka-1 are reporting 34 under-replicated partitions (M1, M2), which is a breach of the normal value of 0 (B3, B4). This indicates that the replicas for these partitions are not in sync, likely because the replica on kafka-2 is offline or unable to write due to the disk full condition. This reduces data durability for the affected partitions.
findings.confirm_by: Check the ISR (In-Sync Replicas) status for the affected partitions to confirm that kafka-2 is out of the ISR set.

recommendations.title: Free up disk space on aks-kafka-pool-0002
recommendations.rationale: The disk is full, causing Kafka to fail. Freeing space is the immediate step to restore the broker's ability to write data and rejoin the cluster.

recommendations.title: Review retention policies and disk capacity planning
recommendations.rationale: The disk filled up rapidly. Reviewing retention settings and ensuring adequate disk capacity or faster cleanup mechanisms can prevent recurrence.

recommendations.title: Monitor ISR status after disk cleanup
recommendations.rationale: After freeing space, monitor the Under-Replicated Partitions metrics on kafka-0 and kafka-1 to ensure they return to 0 as kafka-2 rejoins the ISR.

rca-fd-exhaustion.summary: Kafka broker kafka-2 is experiencing a file descriptor exhaustion event, leading to connectivity failures and high network processor load. The root cause is identified as 'Too many open files' errors starting at 02:11Z, which prevented new connections from being accepted, causing failed produce requests and network saturation. This is a critical availability issue for kafka-2.

findings.title: File Descriptor Exhaustion on kafka-2
findings.detail: The primary cause of the incident is the exhaustion of file descriptors on broker kafka-2. At 02:11Z, the broker began logging 'Too many open files' errors (L1), indicating it could no longer accept new TCP connections. This directly caused the subsequent spike in failed produce requests (M1, B1) and the saturation of network processors (M2, B2) as existing connections were stressed or dropped. The 'Connectivity problem' (P1) is a downstream effect of the broker's inability to handle new connections.
findings.confirm_by: Check the current open file count on kafka-2 (e.g., `lsof -p <pid> | wc -l` or `/proc/<pid>/fd`) against the system limit (`ulimit -n`). Verify if the count is at or near the limit. Also, check if the number of active connections or open segments has grown unexpectedly.

findings.title: High Failed Produce Requests on kafka-2
findings.detail: Produce requests are failing at a rate of ~28/sec on kafka-2 (M1, B1). This is a direct consequence of the file descriptor exhaustion, as the broker cannot accept new connections or process requests on existing ones effectively. This impacts data ingestion for topics served by kafka-2.
findings.confirm_by: Monitor the FailedProduceRequestsPerSec metric. It should drop to zero once the file descriptor issue is resolved.

findings.title: Network Processor Saturation on kafka-2
findings.detail: The network processor idle percentage on kafka-2 has dropped to 0.071 (M2, B2), well below the healthy threshold of 0.3. This indicates the network threads are overwhelmed, likely due to the churn of connection attempts and errors caused by the file descriptor limit. This saturation further degrades performance and contributes to the failed requests.
findings.confirm_by: Monitor NetworkProcessorAvgIdlePercent. It should recover to >0.3 after the file descriptor issue is resolved.

recommendations.title: Increase File Descriptor Limit on kafka-2
recommendations.rationale: The immediate cause of the outage is hitting the OS file descriptor limit. Increasing the `ulimit -n` (or equivalent systemd limit) for the Kafka process on kafka-2 will allow it to accept more connections and open more files (segments, logs). This is a standard mitigation for 'Too many open files' errors.

recommendations.title: Investigate Connection Leak or High Connection Count
recommendations.rationale: While increasing the limit is a quick fix, it is crucial to determine why the file descriptor count spiked. Check for a connection leak (e.g., clients not closing connections properly) or an unexpected surge in client connections. Review recent deployments or client behavior changes around 02:11Z.

recommendations.title: Review Kafka Broker Configuration for Connection Limits
recommendations.rationale: Ensure that Kafka's `max.connections` and `max.connections.per.ip` settings are appropriate for the expected load and do not conflict with the OS limits. If the OS limit is raised, ensure Kafka is configured to utilize the available resources without overwhelming the network threads.

rca-follower-lag.summary: The cluster is experiencing a critical durability issue on broker kafka-1, where partitions are under-min-ISR, causing producer failures for `acks=all` clients. This started around 02:15Z with under-replicated partitions, escalating to under-min-ISR at 02:50Z. The root cause is likely a follower replica falling behind or becoming unreachable, leading to ISR shrinkage. No other systemic issues (disk, GC, controller stability) are evident.

findings.title: Follower replica lag or failure causing ISR shrinkage on kafka-1
findings.detail: Under-replicated partitions (M2) appeared at 02:15Z, followed by under-min-ISR partitions (M1) at 02:50Z. The error logs (L1) confirm `NotEnoughReplicasException` for `payments` partitions, indicating the ISR set size dropped below `min.insync.replicas` (likely 2). This sequence suggests a follower replica (not kafka-1) stopped fetching or became unreachable, causing the leader (kafka-1) to shrink the ISR. The `Unexpected error from /<ip>` logs (L2) on kafka-1 around the same time may indicate network issues or client disconnections related to this follower.
findings.confirm_by: Check the `ReplicaFetcherLag` or `ReplicaManager` metrics for the follower brokers (kafka-0, kafka-2) to see if one stopped fetching or had high lag starting around 02:15Z. Also, check network metrics between kafka-1 and the other brokers for packet loss or latency spikes.

findings.title: Producer failures due to under-min-ISR partitions
findings.detail: Broker kafka-1 has 3 partitions under `min.insync.replicas` (M1, B1). This causes `acks=all` producers to fail with `NotEnoughReplicasException` (L1). This is a direct impact on data durability and availability for the `payments` topic.
findings.confirm_by: Monitor producer error rates for the `payments` topic. The Davis problem P1 (Failure rate increase) likely correlates with these producer failures.

findings.title: Under-replicated partitions persisting on kafka-1
findings.detail: Broker kafka-1 has 12 under-replicated partitions (M2, B2) that have persisted since 02:15Z. This indicates that at least one replica for these partitions is not caught up with the leader. This is the precursor to the under-min-ISR state.
findings.confirm_by: Identify which partitions are under-replicated and which brokers are the lagging followers. Check if these followers are healthy and fetching.

recommendations.title: Investigate follower replica health and network connectivity
recommendations.rationale: The root cause is likely a follower replica failing to keep up. Identifying the specific broker and reason (disk, network, process) is critical to restoring ISR.

recommendations.title: Review `min.insync.replicas` configuration for `payments` topic
recommendations.rationale: If the cluster cannot tolerate a single broker failure, consider if `min.insync.replicas=2` is appropriate for the current topology and SLA. However, fixing the underlying replica issue is preferred.

rca-gc-pause.summary: Kafka broker kafka-1 is experiencing severe response time degradation caused by excessive JVM Garbage Collection (GC) pauses. GC suspension time spiked to ~27% starting at 02:30Z, which saturated request handlers (idle dropped to ~10%) and caused request queues to back up. This is an isolated incident on kafka-1; other brokers and replication metrics are healthy.

findings.title: JVM GC Pressure on kafka-1 causing request handler saturation
findings.detail: The root cause is excessive JVM Garbage Collection activity on broker kafka-1. GC suspension time departed from baseline at 02:30Z, reaching a worst-case of 27.28% (B1). This pause time directly starved the request processing threads, causing the Request Handler Idle Percent to drop to 0.107 (B2) and the Request Queue Size to spike by 290% (M3) starting at 02:50Z. The resulting inability to process requests in a timely manner triggered the 'Response time degradation' problem (P1) at 03:00Z. The issue is isolated to kafka-1, as other brokers' GC and handler metrics remain quiet.
findings.confirm_by: Inspect kafka-1 GC logs (gc.log) for Full GC events or long Young GC pauses around 02:30Z. Check if a recent deployment, configuration change, or specific heavy-load topic partition assignment occurred on kafka-1 just prior to the spike. Verify heap usage metrics for kafka-1 to see if it is hitting

findings.title: Request Handler Saturation on kafka-1
findings.detail: Request handlers on kafka-1 are effectively saturated, with idle time dropping to 10.7% (B2). This is a direct consequence of the GC pauses (M1) preventing threads from returning to the pool. The Request Queue Size (M3) has increased significantly, indicating that incoming requests are waiting for processing. This saturation is the immediate mechanism causing the response time degradation (P1).
findings.confirm_by: Monitor the Request Queue Size and Handler Idle Percent on kafka-1. If GC pauses are resolved, these metrics should recover. If they remain high despite normal GC, investigate for thread deadlocks or specific slow requests (e.g., large fetches) blocking the handlers.

recommendations.title: Investigate and Tune JVM Heap/GC on kafka-1
recommendations.rationale: The primary driver of the incident is GC suspension time exceeding 27% (B1). This suggests the heap is either undersized for the current load on kafka-1, or the GC algorithm is struggling with the object allocation rate. Tuning the heap size or GC parameters (e.g., G1GC region size, pause time targets) may be necessary.

recommendations.title: Review Recent Changes or Load Distribution on kafka-1
recommendations.rationale: Since the issue is isolated to kafka-1, determine if a specific high-throughput topic or partition was recently assigned to this broker, or if a deployment/configuration change occurred on this node specifically. Rebalancing partitions to distribute load more evenly across the cluster might alleviate the pressure on kafka-1's JVM.

rca-network-flap.summary: The cluster experienced a network connectivity disruption starting around 02:34Z, evidenced by ReplicaFetcher connection errors. This led to a burst of leader elections across all brokers at 02:45Z and subsequent under-replicated partitions on kafka-0, which remain active. The root cause appears to be an external network issue rather than a broker resource failure.

findings.title: Network connectivity loss between brokers causing replication and election failures
findings.detail: The timeline shows ReplicaFetcherThread errors (L1) starting at 02:34Z, preceding the leader election spikes (M2, M3, M4) at 02:45Z and the under-replicated partitions (M1) at 02:55Z. The log template L1 explicitly cites 'java.io.IOException: Connection to <n> was disconnected before the response was read', indicating that brokers lost TCP connectivity to each other. This network flap caused followers to fail fetching data, triggering leader re-elections and leaving partitions under-replicated when the network did not fully stabilize or when the controller attempted to reassign leaders.
findings.confirm_by: Check network infrastructure logs (switches, firewalls, or cloud provider VPC flow logs) for packet drops or connection resets between the broker IPs (10.42.x.x) between 02:30Z and 02:45Z. Verify if any broker restarts occurred during this window (none indicated in metrics).

findings.title: Persistent under-replicated partitions on kafka-0
findings.detail: Under-replicated partitions on kafka-0 (M1) rose to 41 at 02:55Z and remain at 41. This indicates that replicas are not catching up to the leader, likely due to the ongoing or residual network issues identified in the root cause. While under-min-ISR is quiet, the persistence of URP beyond a typical restart window suggests durability is reduced for these partitions.
findings.confirm_by: Monitor if URP count decreases as network stability returns. Check if specific topics or partitions are affected to see if the issue is localized to a specific broker pair.

findings.title: Leader election storm across all brokers
findings.detail: All three brokers (kafka-0, kafka-1, kafka-2) experienced a spike in leader election rates (M2, M3, M4) starting at 02:45Z. This is a direct consequence of the network disconnections causing brokers to be marked as failed or partitions to lose their leaders. The rate remains elevated (last values ~4.7-5.9), suggesting the cluster is still stabilizing or experiencing intermittent connectivity.
findings.confirm_by: Observe if the leader election rate returns to 0. If it remains high, investigate controller logs for repeated broker failure detections.

recommendations.title: Investigate network infrastructure between brokers
recommendations.rationale: The primary evidence points to network disconnections (L1) causing the replication and election issues. Since broker resource metrics (CPU, Disk, GC) are quiet, the fault lies outside the Kafka processes themselves.

recommendations.title: Monitor replication recovery and consider manual intervention if URP persists
recommendations.rationale: URP on kafka-0 is stuck at 41. If the network is stable but URP does not recover, it may indicate a stuck fetcher thread or a need to trigger a preferred leader election or reassignment after review.

rca-oom.summary: Broker kafka-0 experienced a Java heap OutOfMemoryError (OOM) starting around 02:54Z, causing the broker process to become unavailable at 03:00Z. This failure triggered leader elections, resulting in persistent under-replicated partitions on the surviving brokers (kafka-1 and kafka-2) as they attempt to catch up or serve traffic without the failed node. The root cause is memory exhaustion on kafka-0, evidenced by a sharp spike in GC suspension time preceding the crash.

findings.title: JVM Heap Exhaustion on kafka-0 leading to Process Failure
findings.detail: The primary cause of the incident is an OutOfMemoryError on broker kafka-0. The timeline shows GC suspension time on kafka-0 departing from baseline at 02:05Z (M3), reaching critical levels (36.74% suspension) by 02:20Z (B1). This memory pressure culminated in explicit 'Java heap space' errors in the logs at 02:54Z (L1). The process became unavailable at 03:00Z (P1), which directly caused the under-replicated partitions on kafka-1 and kafka-2 (M1, M2, B2, B3) as the cluster lost a replica source. The GC spike preceded the OOM and the availability loss, confirming memory exhaustion as the trigger.
findings.confirm_by: Check kafka-0 heap dump or GC logs for the period 02:00Z-03:00Z to identify the specific object types consuming heap (e.g., large message batches, cache bloat). Verify if a recent deployment or traffic spike to kafka-0 correlates with the memory growth.

findings.title: Broker kafka-0 Process Unavailable
findings.detail: The Dynatrace problem P1 confirms that the Kafka process on kafka-0 is unavailable. This is the direct consequence of the OOM error identified in L1. Until this process is restarted and rejoins the cluster, the cluster is operating with reduced redundancy and capacity.
findings.confirm_by: Verify the status of the kafka-0 process via the orchestration platform or host monitoring. Check if the broker has automatically restarted or if manual intervention is required.

findings.title: Persistent Under-Replicated Partitions on kafka-1 and kafka-2
findings.detail: Following the failure of kafka-0, brokers kafka-1 and kafka-2 have maintained 26 under-replicated partitions since 03:00Z (M1, M2). This state has persisted for over 3 hours, exceeding the threshold for a simple restart recovery (B2, B3). This indicates that the replicas on these brokers are not catching up, likely because the leader for these partitions was on kafka-0 and the data is now unavailable or the followers are struggling to sync from the remaining healthy brokers. This poses a durability risk if another broker fails.
findings.confirm_by: Inspect the replication status of the affected partitions to determine if they are currently leaderless or if the followers are stuck in a 'catching up' state. Check if the data on kafka-0 is recoverable.

recommendations.title: Investigate and Mitigate Memory Pressure on kafka-0
recommendations.rationale: The root cause is heap exhaustion. Before restarting kafka-0, it is critical to understand what caused the memory spike to prevent recurrence. If a specific topic or client is sending excessively large messages, or if a cache configuration is too aggressive, these need to be addressed.

recommendations.title: Restore kafka-0 and Monitor Replication Catch-up
recommendations.rationale: Restarting kafka-0 is necessary to restore full cluster availability and allow the under-replicated partitions to recover. However, this should be done after ensuring the memory issue is understood or mitigated (e.g., by temporarily reducing heap usage or isolating the broker). Monitor the URP metrics on kafka-1 and kafka-2 closely after the restart to ensure they return to zero.

recommendations.title: Review Heap Configuration and Traffic Patterns
recommendations.rationale: The GC suspension time spiked significantly before the crash. Review the JVM heap settings for kafka-0 compared to other brokers. Check if there was an unusual spike in bytes-in or message size on kafka-0 around 02:00Z-02:30Z that could have triggered the OOM.

rca-traffic-surge.summary: The cluster is experiencing a severe performance degradation caused by a sudden, sustained surge in inbound traffic (BytesInPerSec) starting at 02:25Z. This surge saturated the request handler threads across all three brokers by 02:40Z, leading to request queue backlogs and a confirmed response time degradation problem at 03:00Z. The issue is currently active and requires immediate investigation into the source of the traffic spike.

findings.title: Inbound Traffic Surge Saturating Request Handlers
findings.detail: A significant increase in inbound data volume (BytesInPerSec) began at 02:25Z on all three brokers (M7, M8, M9), with rates doubling compared to the prior 7-day average. This surge directly preceded the saturation of request handler threads, which dropped to critical idle levels (<0.11) by 02:40Z (M1, M2, M3; B1, B2, B3). The handler saturation caused request queues to build up (M4, M5, M6), resulting in the 'Response time degradation' problem (P1) starting at 03:00Z. The timeline strongly suggests the traffic spike is the primary cause of the current latency issues.
findings.confirm_by: Identify the specific client applications or topics driving the BytesInPerSec spike since 02:25Z. Check if this correlates with a known batch job, deployment, or external event. If the traffic is legitimate and expected to continue, capacity is insufficient.

findings.title: Request Handler Saturation and Queue Backlog
findings.detail: All three brokers (kafka-0, kafka-1, kafka-2) are currently operating with request handler idle percentages well below the recommended threshold of 0.3 (worst observed ~0.096-0.102). This saturation has led to significant request queue backlogs (up to 78 requests queued), which is the direct mechanism causing the response time degradation. The system is effectively at capacity for handling current request rates.
findings.confirm_by: Monitor if the queue sizes (M4-M6) continue to grow or stabilize. If they grow, the cluster is falling further behind. Check if increasing the number of request handler threads (num.io.threads) or scaling out brokers would alleviate the bottleneck, though this requires careful evaluation to avoid GC

recommendations.title: Investigate and Throttle Source of Traffic Surge
recommendations.rationale: The root cause is a sudden doubling of inbound traffic (M7-M9). Identifying the source is critical. If it is a misbehaving client or an unexpected batch job, throttling or pausing it will restore service. If it is legitimate growth, the cluster needs scaling.

recommendations.title: Evaluate Broker Capacity and Scaling Options
recommendations.rationale: The cluster is saturated (B1-B3). If the traffic surge is legitimate and expected to persist, the current hardware or configuration is insufficient. Evaluate adding brokers to the cluster or increasing the number of request handler threads (num.io.threads) per broker, keeping in mind the potential impact on GC and CPU.
